Case Number: 25NNCV03511    Hearing Date: July 17, 2026    Dept: A

JULY 17, 2026

DEMURRER

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV03511

 

MP:     Defendants Tesla Insurance Services and State National Insurance Company, Inc.

RP:      Plaintiffs Akob Tadevosian and Tamara Tadevosian

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at [email protected] or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS:

 

Akob Tadevosian and Tamara Tadevosian (“Plaintiffs”) allege that on June 2, 2024, Tesla Insurance Services and State National Insurance Company, Inc. (“Defendants”) issued Plaintiffs automobile insurance for three vehicles, which included uninsured motorist bodily injury coverage of $100,000 per person and $300,000 per accident.  (SAC, ¶¶9-10.) On June 19, 2024, Mr. Tadevosian was operating a 2022 BMW 330i and his wife, Mrs. Tadevosian, was the passenger.  (Id., ¶15.)  Plaintiffs allege that their vehicle was stopped when it was struck by an uninsured vehicle.  (Id., ¶¶16-17.)  At the time of the collision, the vehicle was registered to Mr. Tadevosian’s cousin, although he made the lease payments on, insured, and drove the vehicle.  (Id., ¶20.)  Plaintiffs allege that on October 29, 2024, they sent a letter to Defendants regarding the claim and on October 31, 2024, Defendants denied their claim on the basis that Plaintiffs (named insureds) were not the vehicle’s owners.  (Id., ¶¶23-24.) 

 

The Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”), filed March 16, 2026, alleges: (1) Breach of the Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing against SNIC; (2) Breach of Contract against SNIC; (3) Promissory Estoppel against all Defendants; (4) Negligence against Tesla; and (5) Unfair Business Practices in Violation of Business & Professions Code, §17200 against all Defendants. 

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 17, 2026, Defendants filed a Demurrer to the SAC.  On July 6, 2026, Plaintiffs filed an opposition.  On July 10, 2026, Defendants filed a reply.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

The grounds for a demurrer must appear on the face of the pleading or from judicially noticeable matters.  (C.C.P. § 430.30(a); Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d311, 318.)  A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint states a cause of action.  (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.)  The only issue involved in a demurrer hearing is whether the complaint states a cause of action.  (Id.)

 

A demurrer assumes the truth of all factual, material allegations properly pled in the challenged pleading.  (Blank, supra, 39 Cal.3d at p. 318.) No matter how unlikely or improbable, the plaintiff’s allegations must be accepted as true for the purpose of ruling on the demurrer.  (Del E. Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal. App. 3d 593, 604.)  But this does not include contentions; deductions; conclusions of fact or law alleged in the complaint; facts impossible in law; or allegations contrary to facts of which a court may take judicial notice.  (Blank, supra, 39 Cal.3d at 318.)

 

Pursuant to C.C.P. §§ 430.10(e) and (f), the party against whom a complaint has been filed may demur to the pleading on the grounds that the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, or that the pleading is uncertain, ambiguous and/or unintelligible.  It is an abuse of discretion to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is a reasonable probability that the defect can be cured by amendment.  (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1074, 1082.)

 

MEET AND CONFER:

 

C.C.P. §§ 430.41(a) and 435.5(a) require that the moving party meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the demurrer and/or motion to strike. Upon review, the Court finds the meet and confer requirements were met. (See Shilling Decl., ¶¶2-6.)

                                                                                                       

ANALYSIS: 

 

Defendants demur to the Third, Fourth, and Fifth Causes of Action in the SAC on the ground that they fail to allege sufficient facts.

 

A.    Third Cause of Action for Promissory Estoppel – Sustained with Leave to Amend  

 

“The elements of a promissory estoppel claim are (1) a promise clear and unambiguous in its terms; (2) reliance by the party to whom the promise is made; (3) [the] reliance must be both reasonable and foreseeable; and (4) the party asserting the estoppel must be injured by his reliance.”  (Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. (2011) 192 Cal.App.4th 218, 225 [internal quotation marks omitted].) The promise need only be definite enough for the court to determine the scope of the duty and limits of performance to provide a rational basis for the assessment of damages.  (Id. at 226.)  “‘Promissory estoppel applies whenever a promise which the promissor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee or a third person and which does induce such action or forbearance would result in an ‘injustice’ if the promise were not enforced....”  (Id. at 227 [internal quotations omitted].)

 

In the Third Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege they obtained the Policy from SNIC naming Mr. Tadevosian as a named insured, he was involved in the automobile collision, and he made every monthly insurance payment on the vehicle.  (Id., ¶¶60-61.)  They contend that Mr. Tadevosian’s status as the vehicle’s payor/operator independently constitutes an insurable interest.  (Id., ¶62.)   Plaintiffs are informed and believe that Defendants’ inclusion of Mr. Tadevosian as a named insured is affirmation that he had an insurable interest in the vehicle.  (Id., ¶63.)  Tesla, on Defendants’ behalf, promised Plaintiffs to provide automobile insurance for three vehicles, including the subject vehicle, with knowledge that Mr. Tadevosian was not the vehicle’s registered owner.  (Id., ¶64.)  By issuing the Policy, accepting premiums, and providing an insurance card, SNIC allegedly ratified Tesla’s promise and separately made a clear and unambiguous promise to provide insurance coverage, with full knowledge that Mr. Tadevosian was not the vehicle’s registered owner.  (Id., ¶65.)  Plaintiffs allege the promise was clear and ambiguous; Defendants knew at the time of policy issuance that Mr. Tadevosian was not the registered owner, accepted premiums anyways, and never notified him of any coverage defect; and there was no express exclusion from uninsured motorist coverage based on the named insured's status as a non-owner of the insured vehicle.  (Id., ¶67.)  Plaintiffs allege they relied on Defendants’ promises that they would be provided insurance coverage; they reasonably and detrimentally relied as they were named insured and Mr. Tadevosian made timely premium payments; and they suffered in the amount of premium payments made towards the Policy and denied benefits owed under the Policy.  (Id., ¶¶68-70.)  Plaintiffs seek the benefits under the Policy or, alternatively, if the Policy is void due to lack of insurable interest, restitution of all premiums paid.  (Id., ¶71.) 

 

Defendants argue that Plaintiffs cannot base a promissory estoppel claim on preexisting obligations where the parties exchanged consideration.  (Youngman v. Nevada Irr. Dist. (1969) 70 Cal.2d 240, 250 [“[W]here the promisee's reliance was bargained for, the law of consideration applies; and it is only where the reliance was unbargained for that there is room for application of the doctrine of promissory estoppel.”].)  “The purpose of this doctrine is to make a promise binding, under certain circumstances, without consideration in the usual sense of something bargained for and given in exchange. If the promisee's performance was requested at the time the promisor made his promise and that performance was bargained for, the doctrine is inapplicable.”  (Id. at 249.)  Defendants argue the parties bargained for and agreed upon the Policy in exchange for premium payments.  They argue that the fact that the law voids the Policy with respect to the subject vehicle because Plaintiffs lack an insurable interest does not void the fact that the promise Plaintiffs seek to enforce was a bargained for promise.  (Dem. at p.4; Ins. Code, § 280 [“If the insured has no insurable interest, the contract is void.”].) 

 

In opposition, Plaintiffs argue that if Youngman applies, then they are still entitled to allege an alternative claim that provides them with relief for justifiable and detrimental reliance based on Defendants’ promise to insure the vehicle in the alternative. 

 

Here, the parties bargained for the Policy and Plaintiffs made insurance premium payments, which was the performance requested at the time Defendants made their promise and that performance (of premium payments) was bargained for.  While Plaintiffs may be entitled to some sort of claim entitling them to restitution, the promissory estoppel doctrine is not applicable in the context of this case. 

 

Next, Defendants argue that it is the “general and quite well settled rule of law that the principles of estoppel and implied waiver do not operate to extend the coverage of an insurance policy after the liability has been incurred or the loss sustained.”  (Aetna Casualty & Surety Co. v. Richmond (1977) 76 Cal.App.3d 645, 652–653 [explaining the rationale as follows: “The rule is well established that the doctrines of implied waiver and of estoppel, based upon the conduct or action of the insurer, are not available to bring within the coverage of a policy risks not covered by its terms, or risks expressly excluded therefrom, and the application of the doctrines in this respect is therefore to be distinguished from the waiver of, or estoppel to assert, grounds of forfeiture.”]; Dem. at p.5.)   

 

Plaintiffs rely on Dones v. Life Ins. Co. of North America (2020) 55 Cal.App.5th 665.  In Dones, the beneficiary of a deceased county employee sued the county and life insurance company after a denial of supplemental life insurance coverage based on a provision that insurance would not become effective if the employee was not in “active service” on the effective date.  The insured had taken medical leave and died six months later without having returned to work. The Dones Court found that allegations of a life insurance enrollee who received confirmation of her enrollment, had premium payments deducted from her paycheck, and was never informed that there were issues with her enrollment, despite employer County and the insurer’s knowledge of her medical leave, alleged sufficient facts supporting waiver and estoppel to withstand a demurrer.  (Dones, supra, 55 Cal.App.5th at 686-687.) 

 

In making its ruling, the Court of Appeal distinguished Dones from Aetna and various cases cited by the insurer.  The Dones Court stated: “The cases LINA [insurer] relies upon involve plaintiffs’ attempts to obtain coverage under existing insurance policies for claims not covered by the terms of their policies. … Unlike the cases LINA relies upon, the present case does not involve the scope of coverage under an existing insurance policy but rather the question whether the policy ever went into effect. None of LINA's cases involve waiver or estoppel in the context of a condition precedent to operative policy coverage.”  (Id. at 678, 680.)  The Court stated, “Waiver and estoppel are normally questions of fact, and LINA's cases do not support a conclusion that these doctrines are inapplicable in the present case. We decline to hold that principles of waiver and estoppel cannot establish the existence of an effective contract of insurance as a matter of law.”  (Id. at 683.)  

 

Plaintiffs argue that Dones is similar because Defendants issued the Policy, it was in effect at the time of the underlying claim, Defendants accepted premium payments, and Defendants did not inform Plaintiffs that the vehicle listed as insured was not in fact insured despite knowing Mr. Tadevosian was not the registered owner of the vehicle.  However, Dones did not include a promissory estoppel claim but, rather, asserted a claim for breach of contract on the ground that both waived or were estopped from asserting the active service precondition to coverage.  (Dones, supra, 55 Cal.App.5th at 671.) 

 

At this point, the Court cannot ascertain whether Aetna applies to the facts of this case.  A copy of the Policy is not attached to the FAC, such that the Court cannot ascertain whether Plaintiffs are attempting to bring within the policy’s coverage risks that are not covered by its terms or risks expressly excluded therefrom.  However, as alleged by Plaintiffs, “the Policy does not contain any express exclusion from uninsured motorist coverage based solely on the named insured's status as a non-owner of the insured vehicle, and Defendants’ denial was not based on any such written exclusion.”  (SAC, ¶67.)  Taking the allegations as true at the pleading stage, the Court finds that Plaintiffs potentially has a claim that can be alleged in the alternative to a breach of contract claim, but, as discussed above, this claim cannot amount to a promissory estoppel claim. 

 

Finally, to the extent that Defendants argue that they had no way of knowing the identity of the subject vehicle’s registered owner outside of Plaintiffs telling Defendants, such arguments are outside the scope of the pleading.  However, this argument and potentially arguments under Aetna may potentially apply beyond the pleading stage after this cause of action is reframed and at a stage where extrinsic facts and evidence may be considered. 

 

Accordingly, the demurrer to the Third Cause of Action for Promissory Estoppel is sustained with leave to amend so that Plaintiffs may recharacterize this cause of action. 

 

B.     Fourth Cause of Action for Negligence – Overruled

 

In the Fourth Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that Tesla owed Plaintiffs a duty to procure an automobile insurance policy that would actually provide insurance for three vehicles. (SAC, ¶73.)  Plaintiffs allege Tesla breached this duty since, according to SNIC, the Policy did not cover Mr. Tadevosian on the basis that he lacked an insurable interest in the Policy.  (Id., ¶74.)  Plaintiffs allege that due to Tesla’s breach, they were deprived of the Policy’s benefits and suffered damages.  (Id., ¶75.) 

 

Defendants argue that Plaintiffs have not alleged a valid basis for any duty Tesla owed to Plaintiffs.  They argue that based on the SAC’s allegations, Tesla was SNIC’s agent such that Tesla owed its principal SNIC certain duties, but did not owe duties to Plaintiffs. Defendants contend, under Brown v. Guarantee Ins. Co. (1957) 155 Cal.App.2d 679, 688–689, that “only bad faith should be the basis of the insured's cause of action. Bad faith may involve negligence, or negligence may be indicative of bad faith, but negligence alone is insufficient to render the insurer liable.”  (See also Sanchez v. Lindsey Morden Claims Services, Inc. (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 249, 254 “Indeed, negligence is not among the theories of recovery generally available against insurers (See Croskey et al., Cal. Practice Guide: Insurance Litigation 2 (The Rutter Group 1998) ¶¶ 12:818, 11:205, pp. 12C-6, 11-48 to 11-49, rev. #1, 1996)”].) 

 

However, the Court does not read Plaintiffs’ Negligence Cause of Action as narrowly as Defendants.  This claim is not premised upon bad faith or Tesla’s failure to properly investigate claims, unreasonable denial of a claim, failure to pay insurance policy benefits, etc., which would be more akin to a bad faith claim.  Rather, the claim is premised upon Tesla’s obligation to procure valid insurance benefits on Plaintiffs’ behalf and Tesla’s failure to do so. 

 

“California recognizes the general rule that an agent or broker who intentionally or negligently fails to procure insurance as requested by a client--either an insured or an applicant for insurance--will be liable to the client in tort for the resulting damages.”  (AMCO Ins. Co. v. All Solutions Ins. Agency, LLC (2016) 244 Cal.App.4th 883, 890.)  “A broker's failure to obtain the type of insurance requested by an insured may constitute actionable negligence and the proximate cause of injury.”  (Desai v. Farmers Ins. Exchange (1996) 47 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1120.)  “Absent some notice or warning, an insured should be able to rely on an agent's representations of coverage without independently verifying the accuracy of those representations by examining the relevant policy provisions.”  (Clement v. Smith (1993) 16 Cal.App.4th 39, 45.) 

 

Plaintiff bring this cause of action against Tesla for its breach of duty to procure automobile insurance for the vehicle Mr. Tadevosian drove at the time of the subject collision.  In this context, a negligence claim would not justify the sustaining of the demurrer. 

 

Finally, Defendants contend the economic loss rule bars the Negligence claim where Plaintiffs seek to enforce contractual obligations.  However, this argument is premised upon a misunderstanding of the Fourth Cause of Action.  As argued by Plaintiffs: “Defendants are claiming there never was a policy in effect, thus Plaintiffs are alleging a cause of action for negligent failure to obtain insurance coverage because Tesla had a duty to obtain automobile insurance.”  (Opp. at p.8.)  Thus, this cause of action is not based on contractual duties to investigate claims, pay insurance benefits, etc., but is based on the procurement (or failure thereof) of insurance benefits in the first place.  At the pleading stage, Plaintiff may plead alternate causes of action on different theories regarding whether a contract/policy existed. 

 

Thus, the demurrer to the Fourth Cause of Action is overruled.

 

C.     Fifth Cause of Action for Unfair Business Practices in Violation of Business & Professions Code, § 17200 – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

The purpose of the Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”) is to protect both consumers and competitors by promoting fair competition in commercial markets for goods and services.  (Buller v. Sutter Health (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 981, 986.)  Section 17200 defines unfair competition to mean and include “any unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business act or practice and unfair, deceptive, untrue or misleading advertising and any act prohibited by [the false advertising law (§ 17500 et seq.)].”  (Id.)  Since section 17200 is written in the disjunctive, a business act or practice need only meet one of the three criteria, i.e., unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent, to be considered unfair competition under the UCL.  (Id.)   

 

In order to plead a claim under Business and Professions Code § 17200, there must be allegations demonstrating that the Defendants engaged in an unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business act or practice.  (Paulus v. Bob Lynch Ford, Inc. (2006) 139 Cal.App.4th 659, 676-77.)  Further, to plead this statutory claim, the pleadings must state with reasonable particularity the facts supporting the statutory elements of the violation.  (Khoury v. Maly's of California, Inc. (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 612, 619.)

 

In the Fifth Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that SNIC has a custom and practice of placing its own financial interest above the interests of its insureds and investigating claims with the intent to deny coverage.  (SAC, ¶78.)  Plaintiffs contend Defendants’ practices violate Insurance Code, §§ 790.03 and 790.04 and.  (Id., ¶79.)  Plaintiffs claim Defendants’ unfair and unlawful practices include: (a) procuring policies Defendants know will not cover the named insured and failing to disclose at point of sale that non-owner status would result in coverage denial; (b) unreasonably interpreting policies to disclaim coverage simply because named insureds are not the registered owner of a vehicle, even though SNIC accepts, and fails to return, insurance premium payments; (c) acting or failing to act in a manner that deprives named insureds of the policy benefits; (d) engaging in a pattern and practice of acting or failing to act in a manner that deprives its insureds of policy benefits; (e) failing to make a prompt, fair and equitable settlement of insurance claims; (f) engaging in a pattern and practice of failing to conduct a prompt, fair, balanced and thorough investigation of claims made under its policies; (g) engaging in a pattern and practice of failing to diligently search for and consider evidence that supports coverage of claims; (h) engaging in a pattern and practice of failing to give at least as much consideration to the interests of its insureds as it gives to its own interests; (i) engaging in a pattern and practice of placing its own financial interests above the interests of its insureds; (j) investigating claims with the intent of finding a reason to deny coverage; (k) engaging in a pattern and practice of investigating claims with the intent of finding a reason to deny coverage; (l) failing to inform Plaintiffs that Mr. Tadevosian would not be insured since he was not the registered owner; (m) including Mr. Tadevosian as a named insured when Defendants internally purportedly believed he did not have an “insurable interest” in the vehicle; (n) accepting premium payments despite their purported internal belief that he would not be entitled to Policy benefits; and (o) convincing the public that named insureds would be entitled to insurance benefits despite not being the registered owner.  (Id., ¶79.) 

 

Plaintiffs contend that Defendants’ practice of accepting premiums from named insureds while internally treating them as uninsured offends the public policy expressed in Insurance Code § 790.03; is likely to deceive reasonable consumers; and constitutes an unfair business practice as immoral, unscrupulous, and substantially injurious to consumers who reasonably believe named-insured status confers coverage.  (Id., ¶¶80-81.)  Plaintiffs allege, upon information and belief, that Defendants have a custom and practice of placing their own financial interests above their clients, including those for whom it purports to procure insurance coverage, and that this custom and practice entails purposefully procuring automobile insurance policies that do not provide coverage to named insureds who are not owners of an insured vehicle, despite Defendants’ knowledge that (1) the named insured will operate the insured vehicle; (2) the named insured expects and believes they will be covered under the policy obtained by Defendants; and (3) the registered owner is not an insured under the policy.  (Id., ¶82.)  Plaintiffs allege Defendants engaged in unlawful, unfair, fraudulent, and discriminatory conduct, such that they suffered loss of money and property.  (Id., ¶¶83-84.)    

 

First, a violation of the unfair prong of section 17200 involves an examination of the impact of the business practice on its alleged victim balanced against the reasons, justifications and motives of the alleged wrongdoer.  (Searle v. Wyndham Int'l (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 1327, 1334.)  An unfair business practice occurs when it offends an established public policy or when the practice is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous or substantially injurious to consumers.  (Id.)  In general, the unfairness prong has been used to enjoin deceptive or sharp practices.  (Id.) 

 

Defendants argue that Plaintiffs have not pleaded specific facts that Defendants knew Mr. Tadevosian was not the registered owner prior to Plaintiffs’ claim.  While the SAC alleges in a conclusory fashion that Defendants knew Mr. Tadevosian did not own the vehicle at the time they issued the Policy, there are no facts supporting this assertion.  (See SAC, ¶22.)  Plaintiffs allege that Defendants engaged in unfair practices by “Unreasonably including Akob as a named insured under the Policy when Defendants internally purportedly believed that Akob did not have an ‘insurable interest’ in the Vehicle.”  (Id., ¶79(m).)   However, there are no facts detailing Defendants’ internal and purported belief that Mr. Tadevosian did not have an insurable interest.  Thus, as currently worded, the Court does not find that Plaintiffs have alleged specific facts showing that Defendants engaged in a business practice that intended to find reasons to deny coverage or included named insureds when they knew the individuals did not have insurable interests. 

 

The SAC fails to identify a particular business practice that offends established public policy or that is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous, or substantially injurious to consumers.  Second, a violation of the unlawful prong includes anything that can properly be called a business practice and that at the same time is forbidden by law.  (Paulus v. Bob Lynch Ford, Inc. (2006) 139 Cal. App. 4th 659, 676-677.) 

 

With respect to Plaintiffs’ citation to Insurance Code, §§ 790.03 and 790.04, these sections cannot constitute a basis for a UCL claim.  As stated in Zhang v. Superior Court (2013) 57 Cal.4th 364, 384: “When the Legislature enacted the [Unfair Insurance Practices Act], it contemplated only administrative enforcement by the Insurance Commissioner. [Citation.] Private UIPA actions are absolutely barred; a litigant may not rely on the proscriptions of section 790.03 as the basis for a UCL claim. [Citations.] However, when insurers engage in conduct that violates both the UIPA and obligations imposed by other statutes or the common law, a UCL action may lie. The Legislature did not intend the UIPA to operate as a shield against any civil liability. [Citation.]” 

 

Next, Plaintiffs cite to California’s Fair Claims Settlement Practices Regulations (10 C.C.R. § 2695.1 et seq.).  However, it is unclear what section of the Fair Claims Settlement Practices Regulation Plaintiffs intend to rely upon.  Section 2695.1 starts with the “Preamble.”  However, Plaintiffs have not cited to a specific portion of the California’s Fair Claims Settlement Practices Regulations or what portion of the regulations was violated.  As such, a review of the pleadings reveals no allegations that identify a law, regulation, or statute and the particular business practices directed at Plaintiffs that violated the identified law, regulation, or statute. 

 

Third, a violation of the fraudulent prong of section 17200 can be shown with allegations that the fraudulent practice was likely to deceive members of the public.  (Schnall v. Hertz Corp. (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1144, 1167.)  The “fraud” prong “is unlike common law fraud or deception. A violation can be shown even if no one was actually deceived, relied upon the fraudulent practice, or sustained any damage. Instead, it is only necessary to show that members of the public are likely to be deceived.”  (Buller v. Sutter Health (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 981, 986.)  A review of the pleading reveals no allegations that identify a particular business practice that was a fraudulent practice likely to deceive the public.  It does not appear that Plaintiffs seek to pursue a UCL claim based on the fraud prong.

 

Thus, the demurrer to the Fifth Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend. 

 

---

THE DEMURRER TO THE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT IS SUSTAINED WITH 30 DAYS’ LEAVE TO AMEND AS TO THE THIRD AND FIFTH CAUSES OF ACTION.   THE DEMURRER IS OVERRULED AS TO THE FOURTH CAUSE OF ACTION.

Case Number: 25NNCV07999    Hearing Date: July 17, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

JULY 17, 2026

DEMURRER; MOTION TO STRIKE

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV07999

 

MP:     Defendants Glendale Unified School District and Theodore Roosevelt Middle School  

RP:      Plaintiffs Raymond Ryan Raffouly and Rita Menasian

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at [email protected] or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Raymond Ryan Raffouly and Rita Menasian (“Plaintiffs”) allege that on February 3, 2025, Theodore Roosevelt Middle School (“TRMS”), Glendale Unified School District (“GUSD”), David T. Beard (“Beard”), Armenuhi Barakezyan (“Barakezyan”), Perla Chavez-Fritz (“Chavez-Fritz “), City of Glendale (“City”), County of Los Angeles (“County”), and State of California (“State”) (collectively, “Defendants”) failed to exercise ordinary care, caution, or prudence to avoid or prevent the accident and that the injuries sustained by Plaintiff was caused by Defendants’ negligence.  Plaintiffs allege that Defendant Employer(s) had independent duties to properly hire, train, and supervise Defendant Employees and that the employees failed such duties. 

 

The Complaint, filed November 12, 2025, alleges a single cause of action for General Negligence.

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 8, 2026, GUSD and TRMS filed a Demurrer and Motion to Strike portions of the Complaint.  On July 6, 2026, Plaintiffs filed an opposition to the demurrer.  On July 10, 2026, GUSD and TRMS filed a reply to Plaintiffs’ opposition to the demurrer and a notice of non-opposition to the motion to strike.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

A.     Demurrer

 

The grounds for a demurrer must appear on the face of the pleading or from judicially noticeable matters. (C.C.P. § 430.30(a); Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal. 3d 311, 318.) A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) The only issue involved in a demurrer hearing is whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Id.)

 

A demurrer assumes the truth of all factual, material allegations properly pled in the challenged pleading. (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at p. 318.) No matter how unlikely or improbable, the plaintiff’s allegations must be accepted as true for the purpose of ruling on the demurrer. (Del E. Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.  App. 3d 593, 604.) But this does not include contentions; deductions; conclusions of fact or law alleged in the complaint; facts impossible in law; or allegations contrary to facts of which a court may take judicial notice.  (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at 318.)

 

Pursuant to C.C.P. §§ 430.10(e) and (f), the party against whom a complaint has been filed may demur to the pleading on the grounds that the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, or that the pleading is uncertain, ambiguous and/or unintelligible. It is an abuse of discretion to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is a reasonable probability that the defect can be cured by amendment. (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles (2003) 31 Cal. 4th 1074, 1082.)

 

B.     Motion to Strike

 

Motions to strike are used to reach defects or objections to pleadings that are not challengeable by demurrer, such as words, phrases, and prayers for damages. (See C.C.P. §§ 435, 436, and 437.) The proper procedure to attack false allegations in a pleading is a motion to strike. (C.C.P. § 436(a).) In granting a motion to strike made under C.C.P. § 435, “[t]he court may, upon a motion made pursuant to Section 435 [notice of motion to strike whole or part of complaint], or at any time in its discretion, and upon terms it deems proper: (a) Strike out any irrelevant, false, or improper matter inserted in any pleading.” (C.C.P. § 436(a).) Irrelevant matters include immaterial allegations that are not essential to the claim or those not pertinent to or supported by an otherwise sufficient claim. (C.C.P. § 431.10.)

 

The court may also “[s]trike out all or any part of any pleading not drawn or filed in conformity with the laws of this state, a court rule, or an order of the court.” (C.C.P. § 436(b).)

 

MEET AND CONFER:

 

C.C.P. §§ 430.41(a) and 435.5(a) require that the moving party meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the demurrer and/or motion to strike. Upon review, the Court finds the meet and confer requirements were met. (Whitmore Decl., ¶¶2-7.)

 

DEMURRER ANALYSIS:

 

GUSD and TRMS to the Complaint on the grounds that it fails to state sufficient facts and is uncertain.

 

A.     Statutory Claim – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

GUSD and TRMS to demur to the Complaint, arguing that Plaintiffs have failed to identify a statutory basis for their claims. 

 

Under the statutory scheme in California, all government tort liability must be based on statute.  (Duarte v. City of San Jose (1980) 100 Cal.App.3d 648, 653.)  Government Code § 815, enacted in 1963, abolished all common law or judicially declared forms of liability for public entities, except for such liability as may be required by the federal or state Constitution.  (Cochran v. Herzog Engraving Co. (1984) 155 Cal. App. 3d 405, 409.)  Accordingly, in the absence of some constitutional requirement, public entities may be liable only if a statute declares them to be liable.  (Id.)  In short, sovereign immunity is the rule in California; governmental liability is limited to exceptions specifically set forth by statute.  (Id.)

 

Further, in order to state a cause of action for government tort liability, every fact essential to the existence of statutory liability must be pleaded with particularity, including the existence of a statutory duty.  (Zuniga v. Housing Authority (1995) 41 Cal. App. 4th 82, 96.)  Since the duty of a public entity can only be created by statute, the statute claimed to establish the duty must be identified.  (Id.)

 

The Complaint alleges:

 

That at said time [02/03/2025] and place of the accident [222 E Acacia Avenue, Glendale, CA 91205] described in the complaint, and that defendants and each of them did not exercise ordinary care, caution or prudence to avoid or prevent the accident described in said complaint, and that said accident and injuries sustained by plaintiff was actually and proximately caused by said fault, carelessness and negligence of defendants and each of them named in the complaint. The Defendant Employer(s) had independent duties to properly hire, train, and supervise defendant employee, and that Defendant employee failed said duties.

 

(Compl. at p.5.) 

 

As currently worded, the Complaint lacks any reference to a statutory basis for Plaintiffs’ claims against a public entity like GUSD/TRMS and merely pleads a common law claim for negligence.  The Complaint also lacks any supporting facts detailing what occurred and how each of the Defendants were involved in the subject incident.  Furthermore, the allegations are not pleaded with the requisite particularity for a statutory claim against a public entity. 

 

In opposition, Plaintiffs argue: “Here, the Complaint alleges that on February 3, 2025, minor Plaintiff Raymond Raffouly was injured at Theodore Roosevelt Middle School when he suffered a fall, injuring his knee and ankle. School personnel were placed on notice of his injuries. Despite having notice that Plaintiff was injured and unable to participate in physical education, Defendant

David Beard required Plaintiff to participate in physical education and complete a 200-meter run. Plaintiff advised Mr. Beard that he was injured and could not participate. Defendants nevertheless required Plaintiff to participate. Plaintiff suffered further injury to his knee and ankle as a direct result.”  (Opp. at p.5.)  None of these “facts” were alleged in the current version of the Complaint.  However, this shows that, upon amendment, Plaintiffs may have additional facts that support their Negligence claim. 

 

The demurrer to the Complaint is sustained with leave to amend.

 

B.     TRMS – Sustained Without Leave to Amend.

 

GUSD and TRMS argue that TRMS is not a separate entity which could be sued as only a school district may be sued. 

 

GUSD and TRMS acknowledge that no California Court of Appeal has addressed the issue, but cites to various federal cases.  (Dem. at pp.7-8; see Lindsey v. Claremont Middle School (N.D. Cal., Jan. 29, 2013, No. C 12-02639 LB) 2013 WL 358173, at *2 [The court further explained that, as Defendants correctly noted in their motion, Claremont [Middle School] is not an entity subject to suit. … Rather, OUSD is the entity that should be named as a defendant to any First Amended Complaint.”]; Doe By and Through Doe v. Petaluma City School Dist. (N.D. Cal. 1993) 830 F.Supp. 1560, 1583 [“Kenilworth Junior High School is not an entity capable of being sued. The entire complaint against it is therefore DISMISSED WITH PREJUDICE.”].) 

 

Education Code, § 35010 states:

 

(a) Every school district shall be under the control of a board of school trustees or a board of education.

 

(b) The governing board of each school district shall prescribe and enforce rules not inconsistent with law, or with the rules prescribed by the State Board of Education, for its own government.

 

(Ed. Code, § 35010.)

 

Education Code, § 35162 states: “In the name by which the district is designated the governing board may sue and be sued, and hold and convey property for the use and benefit of the school district.” 

 

In opposition, Plaintiffs do not oppose TRMS’s dismissal but argue that TRMS’s non-suable status does not defeat a substantive claim against GUSD or warrant GUSD’s dismissal. 

 

Based on the Court’s read of the demurrer papers, the Court understood GUSD/TRMS as seeking TRMS’s dismissal only.  (Dem. at p.8 [“Further, the District’s Demurrer to Plaintiffs’ Complaint should be dismissed as to Roosevelt – without leave to amend – on the basis that Roosevelt is itself, not a suable entity.”].) 

 

As TRMS is an individual department/subdivision of GUSD and is not a separate entity, the demurrer as brought by TRMS is sustained.  As TRMS is not a proper party and the parties do not contest TRMS’s dismissal, the demurrer is sustained without leave to amend.

 

MOTION TO STRIKE ANALYSIS:

 

GUSD and TRMS move to strike the allegations for punitive damages. 

 

“Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a public entity is not liable for damages awarded under Section 3294 of the Civil Code or other damages imposed primarily for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant.”  (Gov. Code, § 818.)  “Government Code section 818 in context means that ... a plaintiff who alleges injury caused by a public entity may be entitled to actual damages for that injury, but not punitive damages. [Citations.]”  (Marron v. Superior Court (2003) 108 Cal.App.4th 1049, 1059.) 

 

“This section was added to the code upon a recommendation of the California Law Revision Commission, which commented, ‘Public entities shall not be liable for punitive or exemplary damages. Such damages are imposed to punish a defendant for oppression, fraud or malice. They are inappropriate where a public entity is involved, since they would fall upon the innocent taxpayers.’ (Recommendations Relating to Sovereign Immunity, No. 1—Tort Liability of Public Entities and Public Employes, 4 Cal.Law Revision Com. Rep. (Jan. 1963) p. 817; see also City of Salinas v. Souza & McCue Construction Co. (1967) 66 Cal.2d 217, 228 [57 Cal. Rptr. 337, 424 P.2d 921].)”  (State Dept. of Corrections v. Workmen's Comp. App. Bd. (1971) 5 Cal.3d 885, 887–888.) 

 

In light of Government Code, § 818 and supporting case law, the unopposed motion to strike the allegations for punitive damages is granted without leave to amend.

THE DEMURRER TO THE COMPLAINT IS SUSTAINED WITH 30 DAYS’ LEAVE TO AMEND AS AGAINST DEFENDANT GLENDALE UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT.

Case Number: 26NNCV01400    Hearing Date: July 17, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

JULY 17, 2026

MOTION FOR PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 26NNCV01400

 

MP:     Plaintiff 13 Splinters dba Stellar Custom Wood   

RP:      Defendant Alex Mendelis

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at [email protected] or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

13 Splinters dba Stellar Custom Wood (“Plaintiff”) allege that in September 2020, Alex Mendelis (“Defendant”) sold all assets of AVM Woodworking, Inc. (“AVM”), including its goodwill, customer relationships, subcontractor network, confidential information, and reputation in the Los Angeles cabinetry market to Plaintiff’s predecessors, Enno and Adrienne Roellgen (“Buyers”).  (Compl., ¶¶2, 16-17.)  As part of the sale, they entered into an Asset Purchase Agreement (“APA”), which included a noncompetition and non-solicitation covenant that the sellers and their affiliates would not directly or indirectly carry-on similar business within 100 miles of the present location of the business (“Covenant”), which applied through September 2030.  (Id., ¶¶20, 22.)  The APA allocated $150,000 of the purchase price specifically as consideration for the Covenant and Defendant was also paid a separate $550,000 consideration for goodwill.  (Id., ¶¶3, 21.)  Following closing, the Buyers continued operating the business and Plaintiff subsequently took over operations as the APA’s successor-in-interest.  (Id., ¶¶24-25.) 

 

Plaintiff contends that after Mr. Roellgen died on May 13, 2023, Defendant reentered the business under the guise of assisting in operations and continuity, gained access to Plaintiff’s pricing models, bidding strategies, and confidential information, and influenced pricing and bidding decisions, resulting in overpriced bids so that Plaintiff lost projects and its reputation was harmed.  (Id., ¶¶27-29.)  Plaintiff paid Defendant approximately $77,780.21 during the transitional period.  (Id., ¶30.)

 

After concluding his transactional involvement, Defendant began competing in the same cabinetry market in violation of the Covenant, such as by acting as a partner/consultant/facilitatory for a competing cabinet shop within the restricted radius. (Id., ¶¶33-34.)  Plaintiff alleges Defendant solicited Plaintiffs’ employees and subcontractors, interfered with Plaintiff’s customer relationships, and caused substantial damage to its goodwill and revenue.  (Id., ¶¶36-42.)

 

The Complaint, filed February 26, 2026, alleges causes of action for: (1) Breach of Contract; (2) Breach of Covenant Not to Compete; (3) Breach of Non-Solicitation Covenant; (4) Breach of Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing; (5) Intentional Interference with Contractual Relations; (6) Intentional Interference with Prospective Economic Advantage; (7) Unfair Competition; and (8) Declaratory and Injunctive Relief.

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Preliminary Injunction.  On July 6, 2026, Defendant filed an opposition.  On July 10, 2026, Plaintiff filed a reply. 

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

“The function of a preliminary injunction is the preservation of the status quo until a final determination of the merits.”  (Beehan v. Lido Isle Community Assn. (1977) 70 Cal.App.3d 858, 866.).  Therefore, a preliminary injunctions may be granted only after the moving party shows there is no adequate remedy at law. (Wilkison v. Wiederkehr (2002) 101 Cal.App.4th 822, 832-833; C.C.P. § 526(a)(4).) “The rule in this state is that injunctive and declaratory relief will not be granted where there is a plain, complete, speedy, and adequate remedy at law.” (Rickley v. County of Los Angeles (2004) 114 Cal.App.4th 1002, 1013 [internal quotations and citations omitted].)

 

“The trial court's decision rests on the consideration of two interrelated factors: (1) the likelihood that [moving party] will prevail on the merits at trial and (2) the interim harm that [moving party] is likely to suffer if the injunction is denied, compared to the harm the [opposing party] is likely to suffer if the injunction issues.” (Perez v. Hastings College of the Law (1996) 45 Cal.App.4th 453, 456 [citing Cohen v. Board of Supervisors (1985) 40 Cal.3d 277, 286].) These factors are applied on an inverse sliding scale: the greater the likelihood of success on the merits, the less that must be shown for interim harm, and vice versa. (Butt v. State of California (1992) 4 Cal.4th 668, 678.)

 

The burden of proof is on the plaintiff as the moving party “to show all elements necessary to support issuance of a preliminary injunction.”  (O'Connell v. Superior Court (2006) 141 Cal.App.4th 1452, 1481.)  Preliminary injunctive relief requires the use of competent evidence to create a sufficient factual showing on the grounds for relief.  (See, e.g., Ancora-Citronelle Corp. v. Green (1974) 41 Cal.App.3d 146, 150.)  Injunctive relief may be granted based upon a verified complaint only if it contains sufficient evidentiary as opposed to ultimate facts.  (CCP § 527(a).)

 

A trial court has broad discretionary powers to grant or deny a request for a preliminary injunction so long as it does not act capriciously. The court should exercise its judgment in favor of the party most likely to be injured. (Robbins v. Superior Court (1985) 38 Cal.3d 199, 205.) If the denial of an injunction would result in great harm to the plaintiff, and the defendant would suffer little harm if it were granted, then it is an abuse of discretion to fail to grant the preliminary injunction. (Id.)

 

EVIDENTIARY OBJECTIONS:

 

With the opposition, Defendant submitted the following evidentiary objections to Plaintiff’s evidence.  The Court rules as follows:

 

·         Adrienne Roellgen’s Declaration: Objection Nos. 2, 3-5, 7-19 are overruled.  Objection Nos. 1 and 6 to portions of paragraphs 33 and 50 are sustained.  

·         Carlos Quintanilla’s Declaration: Objection Nos. 1-2 are overruled.

·         Jesus Magana’s Declaration: Objection Nos. 1, 2, 4, and 5 to paragraphs 4 and 7 are overruled.  Objection Nos. 3 is sustained.

 

ANALYSIS:

 

Plaintiff seeks a preliminary injunction restraining Defendant and all persons acting in concert with him, to be restrained and enjoined, pending final judgment, from directly or indirectly:

 

1. Carrying on or assisting any person or entity in carrying on a business similar to the custom cabinetry and millwork business formerly operated as AVM Woodworking, Inc. (“AVM”) within 100 miles of AVM’s former business location;

 

2. Soliciting or hiring any employees or subcontractors who worked for AVM as of the date of sale or for Plaintiff after succession;

 

3. Soliciting or selling to any customers of AVM as of the date of sale or to any customers of Plaintiff after succession; and

 

4. Interfering with Plaintiff’s goodwill, business relations, economic expectancies, workforce, subcontractor network, or marketplace position during the term of the noncompetition covenant (the “Covenant”), which extends through September 2030.

 

A.     Probability of Success on the Merits

 

The elements for breach of contract are: “(1) the existence of the contract, (2) plaintiff's performance or excuse for nonperformance, (3) defendant's breach, and (4) the resulting damages to plaintiff.”  (Oasis West Realty, LLC v. Goldman (2011) 51 Cal.4th 811, 821.) 

 

Business & Professions Code, § 16601 states in relevant part:

 

Any person who sells the goodwill of a business, or any owner of a business entity selling or otherwise disposing of all of his or her ownership interest in the business entity, or any owner of a business entity that sells (a) all or substantially all of its operating assets together with the goodwill of the business entity, (b) all or substantially all of the operating assets of a division or a subsidiary of the business entity together with the goodwill of that division or subsidiary, or (c) all of the ownership interest of any subsidiary, may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business within a specified geographic area in which the business so sold, or that of the business entity, division, or subsidiary has been carried on, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the goodwill or ownership interest from the buyer, carries on a like business therein.

 

In Alliant Ins. Services, Inc. v. Gaddy (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 1292, the defendant agreed to a noncompetition covenant, which expressly defined the restricted territory as to 58 counties in the State of California.  The Court of Appeal did found this noncompetition covenant valid, reasoning:

 

Thus, California's public policy affirms a person's right to pursue the lawful occupation of his or her choice. […] An exception exists for a noncompetition covenant in connection with the sale of a business, pursuant to section 16601 […].

 

The reason for this exception to the general rule against noncompetition covenants is to prevent the seller from depriving the buyer of the full value of its acquisition, including the sold company's goodwill. [Citation.] “It was the policy of the [common] law, within reasonable limits, to protect the purchaser in the enjoyment of the good will which he had purchased and paid for.” [Citation.] The sold business's goodwill is the “ ‘ “expectation of ... that patronage which has become an asset of the business.” ’ ” [Citation.] The geographic scope of a noncompetition covenant must be limited to the area where the sold company carried on business because “[o]therwise, a seller could be barred from engaging in its business in places where it poses little threat of undercutting the company it sold to the buyer.” [Citation.]

 

(Alliant Ins. Services, Inc. v. Gaddy (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 1292, 1300–1301 [internal quotation marks and citations omitted].)  

 

With respect to the non-solicitation covenant, the Court of Appeal stated that the covenant is permissible if it prohibits the seller from soliciting the seller's clients but is not permissible if it prohibits the seller from soliciting the buyer's clients because: (1) the rationale for enforcing non-solicitation covenants—i.e., they prevent the seller from depriving the buyer of the full value of its acquisition, including the sold company's goodwill—does not extend to the buyer's other customers; and (2) the seller presumably knows who its own clients are but does not necessarily know who the buyer's other clients are.  (Id. at 1306; see also Strategix, Ltd. v. Infocrossing West, Inc. (2006) 142 Cal.App.4th 1068, 1073 [“On the other hand, nonsolicitation covenants barring the seller from soliciting all employees and customers of the buyer, even those who were not former employees or customers of the sold business, extend their anticompetitive reach beyond ‘the business so sold.’ (§ 16601.) They do more than ensure the buyer receives the full value of the business it bought, whose goodwill does not include ‘the patronage of the general public.’”].)

 

Plaintiff argues that it can show the probability of success on the merits because Plaintiff’s predecessors, the Buyers, entered into the APA with Defendant, which included section 19:

 

COVENANT NOT TO COMPETE: Seller [Alex Mendelis] and Seller’s spouse, and their respective Affiliates, individually, shall not directly or indirectly carry on a similar business [X] within a radius of 100 miles of the present location of the Business [AVM] …, solicit or hire any current employees of the Business, solicit or sell to any current customers of the Business or assist anyone else except the Buyer [Enno Roellgen and Adrienne Roellgen] to do so within these limits, or have any interest, directly or indirectly, in such business, except as an employee of the Buyer, for a period of 10 consecutive years from Closing. This covenant shall become an asset of the Business and may be transferred as part of any future transfer of the Business. 

 

(Adrienne Roellgen Decl., Ex. 1 [APA, §19].)  On March 9, 2021, Plaintiff filed a Fictitious Business Name Statement stating that it was doing business as AVM Woodworking, Inc. and/or AVM Woodworking.  (Id., Ex. 2.)  Plaintiff argues that despite the Covenant, Defendant breached the agreement by competing and assisting competitors, soliciting employees and subcontractors, interfering with customers, and misusing confidential information. 

 

Plaintiff provides Adrienne Roellgen’s declaration in support of the motion.  Ms. Roellgen states that after her husband’s death, Defendant temporarily worked inside her business to help with the transition and was paid $77,780.21 for his work.  (Roellgen Decl., ¶¶23, 26.)  She states that Defendant influenced pricing and bidding decisions, made costly errors on projects resulting in financial loss, and steered/diverted work to other cabinet shops for his own benefit.  (Id., ¶¶24-29.)  As part of the sale of the business to Plaintiff, a $130,000 promissory note was executed with a maturity date of September 18, 2030.  (Id., ¶30.)  Following the early payoff of the SBA loan, Defendant asserted the note became immediately due and filed a lawsuit, which was resolved by written Settlement Agreement in April 2025 wherein she paid Defendant $95,000 plus $1,625.01 interest for full resolution of the note.  (Id., ¶¶31-32, Ex. 3.)  She states that pursuant to the Settlement Agreement, Defendant agreed to continue forwarding work to her, but he only forwarded a small project for a single vanity while retaining larger, high value projects for himself.  (Id., ¶¶34-35, Ex. 4.) 

 

Ms. Roellgen states that since that time, she believes Defendant has been actively competing against her business.  (Id., ¶38.)  She states that emails from Julian Sahagun of Lioher Pacific, LLC (a competing cabinetry company) to Defendant’s former business email address identified Defendant as its “partner,” and that Defendant was actively participating in the same type of work and servicing the same customer base that was part of the goodwill she purchased. (Id., ¶¶39-42, Ex. 5 [Dec. 2025 Emails].)  She also provides Defendant’s CSLB listing showing that he is still licensed for cabinet, millwork, and finish carpentry and continues to do business under AVM’s name; he is listed in the Franklin Report (a contractors’ database) with AVM as manufacturers of custom, cabinetry, and millwork in the West L.A., Santa Monica, and Encino areas; and continues to have other cabinetry business advertisement.  (Id., ¶¶43-46, 54-56; Ex. 6 [CSLB License # 400500 for AVM, stating that Defendant certified he owns 10% or more stock in the company], Ex. 7 [AVM’s Franklin Report indicating Defendant as owner]; Exs. 9-11.)  She also believes that Defendant stole or obtained a copy of her Cabinet Vision key (a software platform used by cabinetmakers, millwork shops, and woodworking manufacturers) because she declined his request to let him use her Cabinet Vision key; after July 15, 2025, her key went missing but was still active; and Cabinet Vision sent Defendant an invoice to Defendant’s email on January 27, 2026.  (Id., ¶¶49-52, Ex. 8.) 

 

With respect to employee solicitation, Plaintiff provides Carlos Quintanilla and Jesus Magana’s declarations, Plaintiff’s cabinet maker employees.  Mr. Quintanilla states that over the past two years, Defendant came to the shop many times to ask questions about the work they were doing and if they were working overtime.  (Quintanilla Decl. at 1:19-21.)  He states that he was contacted by Julian Sahagun and offered work but declined the offer.  (Id. at 1:22-23.)  He states that in November 2025, Defendant called him many times but he did not answer.  (Id. at 1:24-25.) 

 

Mr. Magana states that over the past two and a half years, Defendant asked him and other employees many questions about work, what they were doing, who they were working for, and what jobs they were working on.  (Magana Decl., ¶2.)  Mr. Magana states that in October 2025, Defendant came to the shop and asked if he had work and was working overtime, and then Julian Sahagun called and offered him work.  (Id., ¶¶3-4.)  He states Defendant, on one occasion, instructed him to hang his old signs on the building, as well as other maintenance related work, but he refused.  (Id., ¶7.) 

 

With respect to interference, Ms. Roellgen states that her business built cabinetry for Jeff Lewis under a contract entered before Mr. Roellgen’s death, but the project was delayed due to unrelated issues on the client’s end.  (Roellgen Decl., ¶¶65-67.)  When the project resumed, she agreed to lower Jeff Lewis’s prices and his team agreed to pay 100% upon delivery (as opposed to completion) but when the work was nearly complete, payment was withheld because she was told that another cabinetry company would finish the job and she would not be permitted to return to the site.  (Id., ¶¶68-70.)  Lewis’s team included Tyler Myerkorth, who was referenced in the email attached to Exhibit 5 connecting Defendant to Lewis.  (Id., ¶73) 

 

Ms. Roellgen also states that JAG Construction used to be her largest client but, after following Defendant’s bidding advice, she stopped winning JAG contracts.  (Id., ¶¶74-75.)  For example, she states that on the Marguerita Project, Defendant advised and she issued a changer order to increase the contract price by $56,000, which JAG rejected, such that she lost the bid.  (Id., ¶77.)  She states that after this incident, her relationship with JAG changed and she thereafter learned that Defendant actively worked with and assisted other cabinetry companies.  (Id., ¶¶78-79.)

 

In opposition, Defendant argues that Plaintiff has not established its burden because its theory depends on speculation instead of competent evidence and Plaintiff’s evidence is contradicted by sworn testimony. In his declaration, Defendant states that when he entered the APA in 2020, he was 73 years old and sold the business for health reasons with the intention to retire.  (Def. Decl., ¶¶6-7.)  He states that since the sale, he retired from the cabinetry and woodworking industry and has no interest or intent to return to or operate a cabinetry business.  (Id., ¶¶8-10.)  He states after Mr. Roellgen’s passing, he temporarily assisted Ms. Roellgen and the business for a limited period but did not intend to return to the business.  (Id., ¶¶11-12.)  He states that during the temporary transitional period, he never assumed responsibility, control, or influence over Plaintiff’s business, pricing, or bidding; and never diverted Plaintiff’s work to other shops for his benefit, never told customers not to use Plaintiff, etc.  (Id., ¶¶16-35.)  He states that he never solicited Plaintiff’s employees, asked them to leave, or offered them employment; he never asked Mr. Sahagun to contact or offer employment to Plaintiff’s employees; never asked others to take work away from Plaintiff; never treated Plaintiff’s employees as his employees; and did not benefit from any temporary work that Mr. Magana may have performed for Lioher.  (Id., ¶¶36-62.) 

 

Defendant further states that he had no partnership with Lioher and was never Mr. Sahagun’s business partner and that he never diverted or solicited Mr. Lewis, Mr. Meyerkorth, or JAG not to use Plaintiff.  (Id., ¶¶63-98.)  He states that he never stole, took, copied, or used Plaintiff’s Cabinet Vision key, nor has he stolen, retained, or misused Plaintiff’s confidential information.  (Id., ¶¶99-111.)  Defendant states that he never used any former AVM-related email account to secretly divert Plaintiff’s customers or business opportunities, he never used the accounts to misrepresent himself or obtain Plaintiff’s confidential information, etc.; he also points out that Plaintiff acknowledges it had access to these accounts and was able to monitor Defendant’s email.  (Id., ¶¶112-127.)  Since retirement, Defendant has not employed anyone, operated a competing shop, or used Plaintiff’s labor force, customer list, subcontractor list, pricing/bidding information, or trade secrets.  (Id., ¶¶128-135.)  He denies that he caused Plaintiff’s revenue decline or business difficulties.  (Id., ¶¶136-145.)  Finally, he states that he never interfered with Plaintiff’s contracts or prospective economic relationships; never solicited Plaintiff’s employees, customers, and subcontractors; never diverted Plaintiff’s work; never stole Plaintiff’s software key; never misused Plaintiff’s confidential information; never accessed Plaintiff’s private files; never used Plaintiff’s goodwill to compete; and never assisted Mr. Sahagun or any other person in violating Plaintiff’s rights.  (Id., ¶¶146-157.) 

 

David Neiyer, Defendant’s accountant/bookkeeper/tax preparer, has provided Defendant services since 2017 and states that he has not seen any income, payments, deposits, etc. showing Defendant received payment for cabinetry work after he sold his business.  (Neiyer Decl., ¶¶2, 5.)  He has not seen records showing Defendant operated or received income for a cabinetry business after he sold his company, or that Defendant received payment from JAG, Jeff Lewis, Tyler Myerkorth/Meyercourth, Sim Club or any related project, or Lioher. (Id., ¶¶6-10, 18.)  Based on his review of Defendant’s financial and accounting records, he has no records that Defendant had any ownership distributions, partner draws, income, etc. from Lioher; that he had any employees, payroll, subcontractor payments, etc.; that he received income from Plaintiff’s customers, subcontractors, or employees; received money diverted from Plaintiff’s cabinetry work; or any records reflecting that he actively operated a competing business.  (Id., ¶¶11-17.) 

 

Jeffrey Thomas Lewis states in his declaration that from 2018 to 2020, he contracted with Defendant and/or AVM for cabinetry work and believed Defendant had retired from the cabinetry business in 2020 after selling his business.  (Lewis Decl., ¶¶3-5.)  He states that since Defendant retired and sold his business, he has not contacted Defendant for cabinetry work, Defendant has not contacted him regarding cabinetry work, Defendant has not performed cabinetry work for him since 2020, and since 2020 Defendant has not been involved in any of his projects.  (Id., ¶¶6-9.)  He states that Defendant did not solicit him to stop working with, to move away from, or not to use Plaintiff or Ms. Roellgen, nor did Defendant interfere with any relationship, communication, dispute, or issue between himself and Plaintiff or Ms. Roellgen.  (Id., ¶¶10-13.)  He states that any issue, dispute, or decision involving himself and Plaintiff or Ms. Roellgen did not involve Defendant; he did not authorize Defendant to act on his behalf in connection with any cabinetry project after he retired/sold the business; and he is not aware of any facts showing Defendant diverted, interfered with, or participated in any cabinetry project involving Lewis after Defendant retired and sold his business.  (Id., ¶¶14, 17, 18.)

 

Julian Sahagun, Lioher Pacific, LLC’s (“Lioher”) owner/operator, addresses his relationship with Defendant, his limited use of Plaintiff’s employee, and his communication with Tyler Meyercourth:

 

·         Mr. Sahagun states that Defendant is not Lioher’s owner, member, officer, manager, employee, agent, or business partner; Defendant has no ownership interest in Lioher; and Defendant does not control, direct sales activities, direct employees, or have authority to make decisions on Lioher’s behalf.  (Sahagun Decl., ¶¶4-6.)  He only referred to Defendant as his “partner” in a casual/social sense since they play golf together, but Defendant is not his business/legal partner or Lioher’s agent such that any implication that Defendant is his business partner in Lioher is incorrect.  (Id., ¶¶7-8, 41.) 

 

·         Mr. Sahagun states he did not act under Defendant’s direction when communicating with Plaintiff’s employees, Defendant never provided him with employee/customer lists, Defendant never asked him to obtain confidential information from Plaintiff’s employees, and Defendant never asked him to contact Plaintiff’s employees for the purpose of causing them to leave.  (Id., ¶¶9-13.)  In October 2025, Mr. Sahagun’s salesperson, Franco Jimenez, visited Stellar Woodworking to maintain business relationships (not at Defendant’s direction) and Mr. Franco reported that a Stellar employee asked about available work, Mr. Sahagun told Mr. Franco not to offer any work, and Mr. Franco again reported the same employee asking for work two weeks later.  (Id., ¶¶14-19, 48.)  Mr. Sahagun spoke with Jesus Magana directly (with no involvement from Defendant), had known Mr. Magana from prior years working with Defendant, and allowed him to perform limited part-time work for Lioher on four occasions in October and November 2025 after his regular workday.  (Id., ¶¶20-25, 28-30, 47, 49; Ex. A [Check].)  Mr. Sahagun states that Mr. Magana did not perform well so he did not continue using him, and he did not ask Mr. Magana to quit his job, did not offer him permanent or full-time employment, did not ask him to bring any coworkers, and did not ask for confidential information.  (Id., ¶¶26-27.)

 

·         In December 2025, Tyler Meyercourth contacted Mr. Sahagun regarding Lioher’s Artika collection and asked for input regarding the use of panels for an indoor golf/simulator club project and, because he played golf socially with Defendant, he invited Defendant to look at the indoor golf concept from a social/golf perspective.  (Id., ¶¶32-35.)  He understood that Mr. Meyercourth sent certain plans/information to Defendant because he had asked Mr. Meyercourth to involve Defendant in their discussion, but Defendant was not involved as Lioher’s contractor, cabinetmaker, installer, or business partner; Defendant did not request that information to compete, divert work away from, or interfere with Plaintiff; and Defendant did not use the plans to perform cabinetry work.  (Id., ¶¶36-39.)  Mr. Sahagun’s communications with Mr. Meyercourth were based on Lioher’s products and his own interest/knowledge regarding golf and were not intended to divert business from Plaintiff and were not directed by Defendant.  (Id., ¶50.)

 

 

·         He states that he did not conspire with Defendant to divert any customer, project, or opportunity from Plaintiff; he did not request or receive any customer list, project list, drawings, confidential plans, pricing, bid information, trade secrets, or proprietary information from Defendant that belonged to Plaintiff; and he did not use any information from Defendant to solicit Plaintiff’s customers, employees, subcontractors, or projects.  (Id., ¶¶42-44.) 

 

Mr. Meyercourth states that he knew Defendant since 2018 and that the last cabinetry project he worked on with Defendant was in May/June 2023 under contract with Plaintiff.  (Meyercourth Decl., ¶¶3, 5-8.)  He states after that project, he did not work with Defendant and Defendant did not solicit him to stop working with Plaintiff or solicit projects.  (Id., ¶¶9-13.)  He states that he needed wall paneling for one of his jobs and found Mr. Sahagun/Lioher and later learned that Mr. Sahagun and Defendant were friends; Defendant learned about the Sim Club golf project from Mr. Sahagun; and he emailed his renderings to Defendant for personal interest and did not hire him for cabinetry work for Sim Club.  (Id., ¶¶14-18, 20-22.)  He states that Defendant did not try to compete with Plaintiff, did not use Mr. Meyercourth to divert work away from Plaintiff, and did not interfere with Plaintiff’s relationships with Mr. Meyercourth.  (Id., ¶¶23-26.)

 

John Andrews, JAG’s principal, states JAG used Defendant and/or his company for projects before he sold his cabinetry business, but did not continue commissioning or retaining Defendant after he sold the business.  (Andrews Decl., ¶¶4-9.)  Mr. Andrews states that Defendant has not solicited JAG, has not asked JAG to stop working with Plaintiff, has not attempted to divert JAG’s work away from Plaintiff, has not bid on JAG’s projects, and has not performed cabinetry work for JAG.  (Id., ¶¶10-15.)  He states that JAG has not worked with Defendant on cabinetry since he sold his business and has no current business relationship with Defendant.  (Id., ¶¶17-18.)  He states that Defendant did not cause JAG to award cabinetry work to other persons/company’s than Plaintiff, Defendant did not interfere with JAG’s relationship with Plaintiff and JAG’s decision to use/not use Plaintiff was not caused by Defendant.  (Id., ¶¶19-21.) 

 

Based on Ms. Roellgen’s declaration, the Court finds that there may be suspicions or correlations between Plaintiff’s decline in business after Mr. Roellgen passed away and/or Defendant helped in the transition period, but Plaintiff has not shown the likelihood of prevailing at this stage.  Plaintiff has not shown that Defendant breached the Covenant or that Defendant actually participated in a competing cabinetry business.  For example, while she states that Defendant still held himself out with the CSLB and other websites that he owned AVM (now renamed) or performed cabinetry services, she has not shown proof that he in fact continued to conduct such services after he sold his business.  (If anything, it may be that he did not update websites with his business sale or retirement information.) Furthermore, while she “believes” Defendant has been actively competing, she has not shown definitive proof—at most, the evidence provided is speculative and requires inferential leaps. 

 

Next, Mr. Sahagun states that he—not Defendant nor upon Defendant’s urging—contacted Mr. Magana after Mr. Magana sought work with Lioher.  Based on Mr. Sahagun and Defendant’s sworn testimony, Defendant did not solicit employees from Plaintiff and Mr. Sahagun’s use of Mr. Magana four times on a part-time basis will not be imputed to Defendant’s purported solicitation of employees without more.

 

The declarations of Mr. Lewis, Mr. Sahagun, and Mr. Meyercourth also show that Defendant did not solicit their business nor interfere/compete with Plaintiff’s business.  Ms. Roellgen states that she saw declines in business after Defendant’s transitional/temporary work with Plaintiff, but the Court does not find that these conjectures of conclusory statements of belief are sufficient to establish the probability of success on the merits of Plaintiff’s claims. To the extent that Plaintiff contends Defendant indirectly affected the business relationships, here, without more, the Court cannot make such a finding at this time.  Mr. Andrews’ declaration confirms that Defendant did not engage in any cabinetry business since selling AVM. 

 

Finally, Ms. Roellgen states that she has “reason to believe” Defendant stole her Cabinet Vision key because he had asked for it (at an unspecified time) and based on a January 27, 2026 email from Cabinet Vision to Defendant requesting his payment for annual software support.  (Roellgen Decl., ¶52.)  She stated that all emails from the past five years had been sent to her and there is no reason the 2026 email was sent to Defendant.  (Id., ¶53.)  However, this email will not in itself be proof that he stole, had access to, and/or misused Plaintiff’s key. 

 

The Court finds that Plaintiff has not established its initial burden in showing the likelihood of prevailing on the merits of its claims based solely on the evidence presented in connection with this application for a preliminary injunction.  While Plaintiff has presented declaration testimony about suspicions that Defendant engaged in a competing cabinetry business or that he solicited employees, the evidence is tenuous and speculative.  Rather, in opposition, Defendants provides affirmative declaration statements from the various individuals and project-holders that address Plaintiff’s contentions, showing that Defendant did not directly or indirectly compete with Plaintiff or solicit Plaintiff’s customers, business opportunities, employees, subcontractors, etc. 

 

Thus, the motion for preliminary injunction is denied.

 

B.     Balance of Harms

 

Before a court will grant a preliminary injunction, the moving party must establish at least some probability of success on the merits.  (Butt v. State of California (1992) 4 Cal.4th 668, 678.)  “If a moving party is able to make such a showing, a court will then “examin[e] all of the material before it in order to consider ‘whether a greater injury will result to the defendant from granting the injunction than to the plaintiff from refusing it, ....’ [Citations.]”  (Take Me Home Rescue v. Luri (2012) 208 Cal.App.4th 1342, 1353.)

 

“An injunction cannot issue in a vacuum based on the proponents' fears about something that may happen in the future. It must be supported by actual evidence that there is a realistic prospect that the party enjoined intends to engage in the prohibited activity.”  (Korean Philadelphia Presbyterian Church v. California Presbytery (2000) 77 Cal.App.4th 1069, 1084.)  Thus, the threat of “irreparable harm” must be imminent, as opposed to a mere possibility of harm sometime in the future.  (Rutter Guide, Cal. Prac. Guide Civ. Pro. Before Trial (June 2018 Update) Ch. 9(II)-A, §9:508.)

 

As discussed above, the Court finds that Plaintiff has not established the probability of success on the merits, such that the Court need not discuss the balance of harms.
